Integrate a nuisance pool out of a candidate likelihood

Source: R/marginal.R
pool_marginal.Rd

A mechanistic design often splits into coordinates the question is about and coordinates it is not. In the prime-boost application the class coordinate \(g\) and the decay rate \(m_s\) are shared and carry the question, while the per-assay levels \((A_0, C_1)\) and the spike ratios are nuisance: they differ between antigen targets and nothing is being asked about them.

Usage

pool_marginal(loglik, shared, weights = NULL)

Arguments

loglik

A participant-by-candidate log-likelihood matrix, as returned by trajectory_loglik().

shared

A vector of length ncol(loglik) giving the shared point each candidate belongs to. A factor fixes the output column order; anything else is converted with factor().

weights

Optional pool weights, length ncol(loglik), normalised within each shared point. The default is an equal-weight average, which is the Monte Carlo estimate of the integral when the pool is drawn from the nuisance prior.

Value

A matrix with one row per participant and one column per shared point, holding \(\log \overline{p}(Y_i \mid s)\). Column names are the shared point labels.

Details

Those nuisance coordinates must be integrated out, not competed against. If they are left as separate bank atoms, a participant can be matched by any candidate that happens to fit, whatever its \(g\), and the class coordinate stops being identified — a flat trajectory then scores equally well at \(g>0\) and \(g<0\). Averaging instead asks the right question: given this shared point, how well does a typical draw of the nuisance coordinates explain this participant? A flat participant scores badly at \(g>0\) because most of the pool predicts a rise there.

The result is the inner integral of the two-level construction, and is what fit_bank() should be given: the bank's support is the shared grid, not the candidate list.

See also

jitter_marginal() for integrating a calibration offset, fit_bank() for the outer problem.

Examples

ll <- matrix(c(-1, -2, -3, -4, -5, -6), nrow = 2)
pool_marginal(ll, shared = c("a", "a", "b"))
#>              a  b
#> [1,] -1.566219 -5
#> [2,] -2.566219 -6
